evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: The Silver Jubilee Bridge, "Widnes-Runcorn Bridge" or Runcorn Bridge crosses the River Mersey and the Manchester Ship Canal at Runcorn Gap between Runcorn and Widnes in Halton, England.

evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: It is a through arch bridge with a main arch span of 361 yards (330 m).

evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: It was opened in 1961 as a replacement for the Widnes-Runcorn Transporter Bridge, and was initially known simply as the Runcorn Bridge or Runcorn–Widnes Bridge.

evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: In 1975–77 it was widened, after which it was given its official name in honour of the Queen's Silver Jubilee.

evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: It carries the A533 road and a cantilevered footway.

evidence.title: Silver Jubilee Bridge
evidence.text: The bridge is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade II listed building.

evidence.title: Catalyst Science Discovery Centre
evidence.text: The Catalyst Science Discovery Centre (originally known as The Museum of the Chemical Industry) is a science centre and museum focusing on chemistry and the history of the chemical industry.

evidence.title: Catalyst Science Discovery Centre
evidence.text: It is located near Spike Island in Widnes, Cheshire, and next to the River Mersey.

evidence.title: Catalyst Science Discovery Centre
evidence.text: The museum is accredited by the Arts Council England.

evidence.title: Mersey Gateway
evidence.text: The Mersey Gateway is a multi-million pound transport scheme between Runcorn and Widnes in Cheshire, England.

evidence.title: Mersey Gateway
evidence.text: The main part of the project is the construction of the "Mersey Gateway" toll bridge that will span the River Mersey and the Manchester Ship Canal.

evidence.title: Mersey Gateway
evidence.text: The crossing, which will have three traffic lanes in each direction, will be located approximately 1.5 km to the east of the existing Silver Jubilee Bridge.

evidence.title: Mersey Gateway
evidence.text: Apart from the new bridge, the project also includes major civil engineering work realigning the existing road network, constructing new interchanges and landscaping 9 km of highway.

evidence.title: Runcorn
evidence.text: Runcorn is an industrial town and cargo port in Cheshire, England, located within the Borough of Halton.

evidence.title: Runcorn
evidence.text: In 2010, Runcorn's population was estimated to be 61,000.

evidence.title: Runcorn
evidence.text: The town is on the southern bank of the River Mersey, where the estuary narrows to form the Runcorn Gap.

evidence.title: Runcorn
evidence.text: Directly to the north across the River Mersey is the town of Widnes.

evidence.title: Runcorn
evidence.text: Upstream and 8 mi to the northeast is the town of Warrington, and downstream 16 mi to the west is the city of Liverpool.

evidence.title: Listed buildings in Widnes
evidence.text: Widnes is an industrial town in the Borough of Halton, Cheshire, England, on the north bank of the River Mersey where it narrows at Runcorn Gap.

evidence.title: Listed buildings in Widnes
evidence.text: The town contains 21 buildings that are recorded in the National Heritage List for England as designated listed buildings. Of these, 5 are classified at Grade II*, and 16 at Grade II; Widnes has no Grade I listed buildings.

evidence.title: Listed buildings in Widnes
evidence.text: In the United Kingdom, the term "listed building" refers to a building or other structure officially designated as being of special architectural, historical, or cultural significance.

evidence.title: Listed buildings in Widnes
evidence.text: Listed buildings are categorised in three grades: Grade I consists of buildings of outstanding architectural or historical interest; Grade II* includes particularly significant buildings of more than local interest; Grade II consists of buildings of special architectural or historical interest.

evidence.title: Listed buildings in Widnes
evidence.text: Buildings in England are listed by the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport on recommendations provided by English Heritage, which also determines the grading.

evidence.title: Cuerdley railway station
evidence.text: One source gives Cuerdley railway station as being on what is now the southeastern edge of Widnes, England, stating that it was located near the then bone works which the 1849 OS Map shows as at the convergence of Moss Lane, the railway, the Sankey Canal, a creek and the north bank of the tidal River Mersey.

evidence.title: Cuerdley railway station
evidence.text: Of these only Moss Lane is no longer readily identifiable on a modern OS Map.

evidence.title: Cuerdley railway station
evidence.text: The authoritative "Disused Stations" website does not include an article on Cuerdley station, however, it does repeatedly use a map which places Cuerdley station some distance nearer Warrington.

evidence.title: Cuerdley railway station
evidence.text: This is corroborated by the Engineer's Line Reference (ELR) database which gives Cuerdley station as 1 mile 10 chains from Fiddlers Ferry and Penketh station and 1 mile 31 chains from Carterhouse Junction.

evidence.title: Cuerdley railway station
evidence.text: Furthermore, the ELR data gives the station site as only 31 chains west of the modern-day junction for Fiddlers Ferry Power station.

evidence.title: River Mersey
evidence.text: The River Mersey is a river in the North West of England.

evidence.title: River Mersey
evidence.text: Its name is derived from the Anglo-Saxon language and translates as "boundary river".

evidence.title: River Mersey
evidence.text: The river may have been the border between the ancient kingdoms of Mercia and Northumbria and for centuries it formed part of the boundary between the historic counties of Lancashire and Cheshire.

evidence.title: Deschutes River (Washington)
evidence.text: The Deschutes River is a 50 mi river in Washington, United States.

evidence.title: Deschutes River (Washington)
evidence.text: Its source is in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest in Lewis County, and it empties into Budd Inlet of Puget Sound at Olympia in Thurston County.

evidence.title: Deschutes River (Washington)
evidence.text: It was given its name by French fur traders, who called it Rivière des Chutes, or "River of the Falls", a translation of the First Nations name for the site.

evidence.title: Deschutes River (Washington)
evidence.text: (The city of Tumwater, founded in the same location, takes its name from another translation for "waterfall", this one in Chinook Jargon.)

evidence.title: Fiddlers Ferry power station
evidence.text: Fiddlers Ferry Power Station is a coal fired power station located in Warrington, Cheshire, in North West England, which is capable of co-firing biomass.

evidence.title: Fiddlers Ferry power station
evidence.text: It is situated on the north bank of the River Mersey between the towns of Widnes and Warrington.

evidence.title: Fiddlers Ferry power station
evidence.text: Opened in 1971, the station has a generating capacity of 1,989 megawatts (MW).

evidence.title: Fiddlers Ferry power station
evidence.text: In a bid to combine efforts at the design and construction stages the Boiler and Turbo-generator plant were replicated at West Burton power station located between Retford and Gainsborough in North Nottinghamshire.

evidence.title: Lac qui Parle River
evidence.text: The Lac qui Parle River is a tributary of the Minnesota River, 118 miles (190 km) long, in southwestern Minnesota in the United States.

evidence.title: Lac qui Parle River
evidence.text: A number of tributaries of the river, including its largest, the West Branch Lac qui Parle River, also flow in eastern South Dakota.

evidence.title: Lac qui Parle River
evidence.text: Via the Minnesota River, the Lac qui Parle River is part of the watershed of the Mississippi River, draining an area of 1,156 sqmi in an agricultural region.

evidence.title: Lac qui Parle River
evidence.text: Slightly more than two-thirds of the Lac qui Parle watershed is in Minnesota.

evidence.title: Lac qui Parle River
evidence.text: "Lac qui parle" means "the lake which speaks" in the French language, and was a translation of the Sioux name for Lac qui Parle, a lake on the Minnesota River upstream of the mouth of the Lac qui Parle River.
